questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has had colicky periumbilical pain and vomiting since yesterday. She mentions one episode of diarrhoea yesterday lunchtime and says she has not opened her bowels since. You are taking a focused history in the ED. Which question best tells you whether her obstruction is complete?
options: "Has there been any blood or mucus in your bowel motions?"
"Have you passed any wind from your back passage since then?"
"Have you noticed any change in your bowel habit in recent months?"
"Have you had any pain or straining when opening your bowels?"
questions.why: Absolute constipation means no stool and no flatus. Patients rarely mention wind unless asked, and passing no flatus points to complete obstruction. An early episode of diarrhoea is common in SBO as the bowel beyond the blockage empties.
notes: Blood or mucus helps screen for colitis, ischaemia or malignancy, but it does not tell you whether the obstruction is complete.
A change in bowel habit over months screens for colorectal malignancy, but it does not tell you whether gas is getting past the blockage now.
Tenesmus or painful defecation points to a rectal or anal cause and does not tell you whether the obstruction is complete.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has a high-grade adhesive small bowel obstruction on CT. She is nil by mouth, has an NG tube on free drainage and IV fluids running, and is still very nauseated. Which antiemetic order is most appropriate?
options: Ondansetron 4 mg as an orally disintegrating wafer
questions.why: In mechanical bowel obstruction, use a non-prokinetic antiemetic given parenterally. IV ondansetron 4 mg is a standard choice for an adult who is nil by mouth and vomiting.
notes: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and is contraindicated in mechanical bowel obstruction, because it increases peristalsis against the blockage.
Domperidone is also a prokinetic, and an oral drug is unsuitable for a patient who is nil by mouth and vomiting with an obstructed gut.
The drug is fine, but a wafer is still swallowed and absorbed from an obstructed, vomiting gut that is being drained by NG tube, so the IV route is more reliable.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has vomited repeatedly for 24 hours from a small bowel obstruction. Her venous gas shows pH 7.47 and HCO3 32 mmol/L. Na is 133, K 3.2 and Cl 92 mmol/L, and creatinine has risen from 68 to 108 µmol/L. What is the main mechanism of her hypokalaemia?
options: Potassium lost directly in the vomited gastric fluid over 24 hours of repeated emesis
Potassium shifted into cells by insulin release
Faecal potassium lost in the single episode of diarrhoea
Aldosterone-driven potassium secretion in the collecting duct
questions.why: Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone drives distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+ secretion, so most of the potassium is lost in the urine, and the H+ loss helps sustain the alkalosis.
notes: Gastric fluid contains only about 5–10 mmol/L of potassium, so vomitus accounts for a small part of the deficit.
She has not eaten and her glucose is normal, so insulin-driven shift into cells is not the main cause. Alkalosis causes only a modest shift.
One episode of diarrhoea loses too little potassium to explain the deficit, and she has passed nothing since.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, presents with small bowel obstruction. While examining her hernial orifices, you remember that a small femoral hernia in a woman is easily missed and can cause SBO. Relative to surface landmarks, where would you feel for the neck of a femoral hernia?
options: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle, at the superficial inguinal ring
Just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, at the deep inguinal ring
Below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery pulse
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, medial to the femoral vein
questions.why: The femoral canal lies below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, so a femoral hernia sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Inguinal hernias appear above and medial to it. This landmark is how you tell the two apart.
notes: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle is the superficial inguinal ring, where inguinal hernias appear.
The deep inguinal ring lies above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament and is the entry point for indirect inguinal hernias, not femoral ones.
Lateral to the femoral artery is the femoral nerve. The femoral canal is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath.
